sections.skill: Tell requests for facts from requests for invention, and label fiction

questions.prompt: Which request asks for invention?

choices.text: "What year was the first public library opened in our town, according to records?"
"Write a story about a dragon who runs a bakery."

questions.correct_answer: "Write a story about a dragon who runs a bakery."
questions.intro: Some requests ask for FACTS ("When did the library open?") and some ask for INVENTION ("Write a short story about a talking library"). Generative tools are good at invention, but they can blur the line: a story may include real place names, or a "fact" answer may contain invented details. Be clear about which you want. When you ask for creative work, invention is fine, but LABEL it as fiction if others might mistake it for fact. When you need facts, ask for sources and check them. Mixing the two without labels can mislead readers.

sections.skill: Compare a history book with a historical novel

questions.prompt: What does a history book try to do?

choices.text: Report what really happened, with sources
Invent new characters and conversations to make the past more exciting to read

questions.correct_answer: Report what really happened, with sources
questions.intro: A HISTORY BOOK tries to report what really happened, with sources. A HISTORICAL NOVEL may be set in a real time and place but invents characters, conversations and events to tell a story. Both are valuable, and the cover tells you which one you are reading. AI output has no automatic cover: the same tool can write either kind. So you need to know which kind you asked for, and label invented material so readers know too.

sections.title: Apply it

questions.prompt: Someone creates a fake but realistic quote from a real scientist "as a joke." What is the risk?

choices.text: It can spread without its context and mislead people
No risk, because jokes are always understood as jokes by everyone who sees them

questions.correct_answer: It can spread without its context and mislead people
questions.intro: The blur is a real risk with realistic-looking content: a "sample" news article, a fictional quote attributed to a real person, an invented review, or a made-up statistic in a school project. Even as a joke, content that looks real can spread without its context. Good practice: avoid attributing invented words to real people, mark examples as "fictional" or "sample," and never present invented data as real findings.
